situation:
You are the plant operations manager for NORTHFIELD FIXTURE WORKS, a mid-size manufacturer that builds custom display fixtures for retail chains across the region. The vice president of operations (judge) has asked you to recommend how the company's first out-of-state plant should be run when it opens this spring.

NORTHFIELD FIXTURE WORKS has won its accounts on a two-week lead time no regional competitor matches, and store buyers plan their seasonal floor resets around it. The company also follows its own guarding and two-person lift rule on the panel line, stricter than the law requires, adopted after an injury and slowing output by about a tenth.

The expansion budget is thin. Running the new plant on the faster older method would hold the lead time at no added cost, but it would put an unfamiliar crew on the process the company retired. Adding a second shift keeps the rule in place, though it spends money the expansion does not have and could leave the first out-of-state contracts earning almost nothing.

The vice president (judge) wants your analysis of which course the new plant should take and of what its crew and the retail buyers should be told to expect. The vice president (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the vice president of operations (judge) for NORTHFIELD FIXTURE WORKS. Business background is the same as the situation above.

You will greet the participant, ask to hear their ideas, and after the presentation you will ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: A year from now, what will this decision have changed about how the plant works?
